newsitem.title: USA: U.S.-Europe to meet on transatlantic air pact.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Europe to meet on transatlantic air pact.

text.p: Senior U.S. and European Union aviation officials are to meet this week to open what are certain to be long and arduous talks toward ending the many restrictions now curbing transatlantic air travel.

Their aim is eventually to write an "open skies" aviation services agreement that would allow American carriers to fly to any of the 15 EU countries and give EU airlines unlimited access to U.S. cities.

The Washington meetings on Wednesday and Thursday will be the first between the two following an agreement by the EU to allow its executives in Brussels to work out a common aviation policy with Washington.
An overall U.S.-EU agreement would replace the many separate bilateral pacts now governing air services between the United States and Europe.

But no hope was expressed that any early accord was likely, with some European nations still protective of their national airlines and reluctant to see them in unrestricted competition with the generally more efficient U.S. carriers.
A U.S. official said "the aim is for the EU delegation to explain its mandate and to discuss the future of transatlantic aviation."
"These are not formal negotiations," he added.

Transatlantic air travel is now hampered by myriad curbs that limit routes, schedules and fares, and while some EU nations have reached "open skies" pacts with Washington, others are reluctant to cede sovereignty to Brussels.
The United States has argued that a free market in aviation would spur competition and drive down air fares.

EU officials said the discussions with the United States would eventually include open access to each other's markets, but initially talks would be confined to competition rules and investment possibilities.

Some foreign carriers have shown interest in buying a controlling interest in American carriers, but law now bars foreigners from owning more than 25 percent of a U.S. airline, and there is little sentiment in Congress to change that.
The EU action to negotiate as a single entity with the United States follows separate "open skies" accords the United States reached with Germany and some smaller EU members.
U.S. officials said at the time they hoped the separate agreements would pursuade the EU to agree to negotiate with the United States as a single entity.

The EU move to negotiate as a community also followed a spate of separate marketing agreements U.S. airlines reached with European carriers to coordinate their reservation systems, schedules and frequent flyer programmes.
They include pacts between United Airlines, a unit of UAL, and Deutsche Lufthansa; Northwest Airlines and KLM Royal Dutch Airlines; and Delta Air Lines and Swissair, Sabena and Austrian Airlines.
In addition, American Airlines, a unit of AMR, and British Airways have announced plans to coordinate their transatlantic services.
